 Singaporean man extradited to US to face charges in alleged global insider-trading scheme
 Saturday, 21 November 2026, 01:23 
 Illustrative photo. Source: Daderot / Wikimedia Commons, CC0. 
 Zhi Ge was extradited from Singapore to the US to face securities fraud and money laundering charges linked to an alleged insider-trading network. 
 Prosecutors allege that Ge helped lead a global network that made tens of millions of dollars trading on confidential information about the finances and merger plans of numerous companies. He is one of nine people charged with taking part in the alleged scheme, which prosecutors say relied on tips from investment bankers and other corporate insiders over several years.
 This is reported by Reuters .
 Ge, 35, made his initial appearance in federal court in Boston on Friday after being extradited from Singapore. The US Department of Justice said he faces securities fraud and money laundering charges following his arrest in Singapore in 2024. A court there recently ordered his extradition. He is scheduled to appear in federal court again on December 16 for an arraignment.
 Advertisement 
 Prosecutors say Ge led the scheme with Samy Khouadja, a former investment banker in France, and Eamma Safi, who co-owned a French restaurant with Khouadja. The US considers most of the defendants, including Khouadja, fugitives. Safi, who has been in US custody since 2025, has pleaded not guilty.
 “He will plead not guilty and anticipates a vigorous defense,” 
 - Kevin Barron
 Ge’s lawyer, Kevin Barron, said this in an email. A lawyer for Khouadja did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
 Prosecutors allege that Khouadja, Safi and Ge recruited bankers and others from 2016 to 2024 to provide inside information about various publicly traded companies, and paid them for the tips. Charging papers say Ge tried to recruit more insiders. They cite messages he sent in 2019 urging an actor friend in New York to introduce him to “investment bankers in big banks working in M&A specifically.”
 The indictment says the tips enabled trades before announcements about deals, including AstraZeneca’s planned $39 billion acquisition of Alexion Pharmaceuticals in 2020 and Novartis’s $2.9 billion acquisition of MorphoSys in 2024.
 Prosecutors say Ge and others used “burner” cell phones and encrypted messaging apps to conceal their activity, and spoke in code, referring to money as “greens” and prospective merger partners as “girls” and “models.” They also allegedly leaked information they had obtained to journalists so they could profit from trades once the news became public.
